groups.title: Token Authentication Concepts
groups.question: You are adding login and registration to your Django REST API for the React app. Explain the token options and how you would protect the API.

followUps.Token vs JWT Authentication: How does DRF's built-in token auth differ from JWT?
followUps.Login and Registration API Endpoints: What should the login and registration endpoints do?
followUps.Protecting API Views with Permissions: How do you require authentication across the whole API?

evidence.text: DRF's built-in tokens are stored in the database and looked up on each request.
JWTs carry their data and are verified by signature without a lookup.
Simple JWT is the common library for JWT with DRF.
Login checks the credentials and returns a token.
Registration creates a user, often returning a token for immediate login.
Serializers validate input, and passwords are hashed by Django's user model.
Default authentication and permission classes are set in DRF settings.
This protects every view by default.
Individual views can override the defaults, for example to allow public reads.

groups.title: Token Lifecycle Management
groups.question: Your JWTs last 30 days, and when a user logs out their token still works. Explain how token lifetimes and logout should work.

followUps.Access Tokens, Refresh Tokens, and Rotat: Why use short access tokens with refresh tokens?
followUps.Logout and Token Blacklisting: How can you make logout actually invalidate a JWT session?

evidence.text: Short-lived access tokens limit damage if stolen.
A refresh token gets new access tokens without logging in again.
Rotating refresh tokens issues a new one each time, making stolen ones less useful.
A JWT stays valid until it expires.
Storing invalidated refresh tokens in a blacklist stops them being used.
On logout, the refresh token is blacklisted so no new access tokens can be made.

notEnough: Only saying you delete the token.

groups.title: React Auth Implementation
groups.question: On the React side, you need to store the token and let the whole app know who is logged in. Explain your storage choice and how components access the user.

followUps.Storing Tokens: localStorage vs Cookies: What are the risks of storing the token in localStorage versus an HttpOnly cookie?
followUps.Auth Context and useContext Hook: How does an AuthContext share the current user?

evidence.text: localStorage is simple but any script, including injected ones, can read it.
HttpOnly cookies cannot be read by JavaScript.
Cookies are sent automatically, so they need CSRF protection.
A context provider wraps the app and holds the user and token.
Components read it with useContext.
They show or redirect based on whether a user is logged in.

groups.title: Protected Routes and UX
groups.question: Signed-out users can open the dashboard, and when an access token expires users are kicked out mid-session. Explain how you would protect routes and refresh tokens.

followUps.Protected Route Component Pattern: How does a protected route component work in React Router?
followUps.Axios Interceptor for Token Refresh: How would an Axios interceptor refresh an expired token without the user noticing?

evidence.text: It checks the auth state before showing private routes.
If the user is not logged in, it redirects to /login.
With nested routes, it renders an Outlet for the protected pages.
The interceptor catches 401 responses.
It calls the refresh endpoint and stores the new token.
It retries the original request so the calling code never sees the error.

notEnough: Only saying it refreshes the token.
